sources.title: Stephen Jay Gould (Q180619) -- verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-10-23): English label 'Stephen Jay Gould', description 'American biologist and historian of science (1941-2002)', born 10 September 1941, died 20 May 2002, Korean label '스티븐 제이 굴드', P18 image 'Stephen Jay Gould.jpg'. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Stephen Jay Gould' (britannica.com; read via an Internet Archive copy because the live page blocks automated clients), read in full: American paleontologist, evolutionary biologist and science writer; Antioch 1963, Columbia PhD 1967, Harvard from 1967 (full professor 1973); technical work on West Indian land snails; with Niles Eldredge developed punctuated equilibrium in 1972, opposed by many including E. O. Wilson; argued population genetics cannot explain large-scale change such as the Cambrian explosion; later work drew criticism; books Ontogeny and Phylogeny, The Mismeasure of Man (1981), Time's Arrow, Time's Cycle, Wonderful Life (1989); regular essays in Natural History from 1974; president of the AAAS when he wrote Rocks of Ages (1999). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE. Encyclopaedic, with a brief note that much of his later work was criticised.

National Science Foundation press release PR 99-35 (NSB 99-89), 'Public Service Awards Go to Stephen Jay Gould and PBS' Bill Nye, "The Science Guy"' (May 1999; read via the Internet Archive copy of nsf.gov and the Wikimedia Commons image of the release), read in full: the National Science Board names Gould for its second annual Public Service Award, saying his investigations of evolution with Niles Eldredge produced punctuated equilibrium, 'arguably the most significant insight into evolution's mechanisms since Darwin', and that his nearly 20 books, essays, lecturing and teaching and his advisory role on PBS's NOVA served the public understanding of science; committee chair David Perlman describes two fronts of public service. Award-body citation, retrospective and admiring.

Harvard Gazette obituary of Stephen Jay Gould (news.harvard.edu, May 2002), read in full: Gould spent his professional career at Harvard, becoming curator of invertebrate paleontology in 1973 and Alexander Agassiz Professor of Zoology in 1982; colleagues called him 'the bulldog of evolutionary biology' for outspoken advocacy of his views; Richard Lewontin, a friend and colleague of 25 years who taught an evolution course with him, calls him creative and original and the best science writer for the public; Andrew Knoll says his powerful and commonly controversial ideas inspired PhD theses for three decades; wrote on topics from baseball to the Piltdown hoax; National Book Award 1981 for The Panda's Thumb, National Book Critics Circle Award 1982 for The Mismeasure of Man; The Structure of Evolutionary Theory (2002) took more than 20 years. University obituary with friendly colleague quotes; its passages on his health and family are deliberately ignored.

Genome Biology research news, 'Stephen Jay Gould dies' (22 May 2002), read in full: Gould and fellow graduate student Niles Eldredge proposed punctuated equilibrium, a debate that still rages thirty years later; a provocative and controversial thinker and a fierce public defender of evolution; president of the AAAS and member of the National Academy of Sciences; taught at Harvard and NYU; wrote 300 consecutive monthly essays for Natural History. Brief science-news obituary; the cause-of-death sentence is ignored.

Jason E. Lewis, David DeGusta, Marc R. Meyer, Janet M. Monge, Alan E. Mann and Ralph L. Holloway, 'The Mismeasure of Science: Stephen Jay Gould versus Samuel George Morton on Skulls and Bias', PLOS Biology 9(6): e1001071 (June 2011), read in full: the authors remeasured 308 of the 670 skulls whose capacity Morton published and reanalysed Morton's and Gould's analyses; they conclude Morton did not manipulate data, that most of Gould's criticisms of Morton in his 1978 Science paper and The Mismeasure of Man are poorly supported or falsified, and that Gould's own analysis is likely the stronger example of bias influencing results; they note Gould offered a 'plausible scenario' for mismeasurement without remeasuring skulls, say they admire other parts of his work, particularly his opposition to racism, and expect he would have defended his analysis. Adversarial, specialist, post-mortem critique; later commentary disputing parts of it was NOT opened.

The New Criterion, 'The apotheosis of Stephen Jay Gould' (volume 21, number 2, 2002), only the opening paragraphs available without payment (read via an Internet Archive copy): a critical conservative essay arguing his obituaries were out of proportion and that peer opinion of the quality of his thought was divided and negative, quoting John Maynard Smith: 'because of the excellence of his essays' non-biologists see him as the preeminent evolutionary theorist while evolutionary biologists tend to see his ideas as 'so confused as to be hardly worth bothering with'. Opinionated, politically slanted and partly paywalled; used only to document a named critic's judgement, never for dates or scores beyond that.

Wikimedia Commons file pages 'Stephen Jay Gould.jpg' (Lawrence Lipke, 1980 dust-jacket photo, 415 x 564, tag PD-US-dust-jacket with an eBay listing offered as proof of no notice) and 'SJ Gould 1985 Flamingos Smile Jacket Photo by Eric Taylor.png' (Eric Taylor, 1985, same tag and theory, 2920 x 3544), plus the Commons category listing and PLOS Biology's statement that its Gould photo by Kathy Chapman is used under CC BY 3.0 (no Commons or Flickr page for that photo found), checked for portrait rights. Not used for any scoring.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_gould_britannica, src_gould_nsb, src_gould_harvard, src_gould_genomebiology | 1972-2002 | encyclopaedia + award body + university obituary + science news] With Niles Eldredge he proposed punctuated equilibrium in 1972, which the National Science Board called arguably the most significant insight into evolution's mechanisms since Darwin and which Genome Biology says was still debated thirty years on; Britannica adds that he argued population genetics cannot explain large-scale change such as the Cambrian explosion, and Lewontin calls him creative and original. The idea is widely recognised and original, but it was shared with Eldredge, remains contested, and the strongest praise is retrospective, so documented at a moderate-to-good confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 76 / 0.66 lowered to 72 / 0.60 because the strongest evidence is retrospective award language and obituary praise, with the theory's value still disputed.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_gould_britannica, src_gould_harvard, src_gould_newcriterion, src_gould_genomebiology | 1972-2002 | encyclopaedia + university obituary + critical essay + science news] Britannica says punctuated equilibrium was opposed by many, including E. O. Wilson, and that much of his later work drew criticism; Harvard colleagues describe powerful and commonly controversial ideas; Lewontin says he did not reduce evolution to a cartoon; a critical essay quotes John Maynard Smith saying evolutionary biologists often saw his ideas as confused. A consistent record of holding positions against mainstream views, with peers divided on their merit, so documented at a moderate confidence and dual-edged.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_gould_harvard, src_gould_nsb, src_gould_britannica | 1974-2002 | university obituary + award body + encyclopaedia] The National Science Board gave him a public service award for helping the public understand science through books, essays, lecturing and NOVA; Harvard cites the National Book Award (1981) and National Book Critics Circle Award (1982) and Lewontin calls him the best science writer for the public; Britannica describes a graceful, clear literary style and regular Natural History essays from 1974. Broad public influence on how people think about evolution is independently documented, though most of it is retrospective praise from admirers, so documented at a moderate confidence. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): first-pass 74 / 0.60 lowered to 70 / 0.55 because it measures public writing influence and the sources are admiring obituaries and an award citation.

persistence.rationale: [src_gould_genomebiology, src_gould_harvard | 1974-2002 | science news + university obituary] He wrote 300 consecutive monthly essays for Natural History, which Genome Biology compares to a streak of tenacity, and Harvard reports that his 1,433-page The Structure of Evolutionary Theory took more than 20 years to complete. Long, sustained output in two forms is documented; the sources are obituaries and the inference is from output rather than from described setbacks, so a moderate confidence.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_gould_harvard, src_gould_britannica, src_gould_genomebiology | 1970s-2002 | university obituary + encyclopaedia + science news] Harvard colleagues called him 'the bulldog of evolutionary biology' for his outspoken advocacy; Britannica records his theory being opposed by many, including E. O. Wilson; Genome Biology calls him a fierce public defender of evolution. A documented willingness to argue publicly with prominent scientists, from friendly or neutral sources; how he handled specific disputes is not described, so a moderate confidence and dual-edged.

cross_domain_range.rationale: [src_gould_harvard, src_gould_britannica, src_gould_nsb | 1967-2002 | university obituary + encyclopaedia + award body] Harvard says he wrote on topics from baseball to the Piltdown hoax; Britannica lists books on evolutionary biology, intelligence testing, geology and paleontology and a book on science and religion, alongside technical work on land snails; the National Science Board notes contributions to systematics. Breadth across technical paleontology, history of science and public essays is clearly documented; the quality of the cross-domain work is contested, so a moderate confidence.

collaboration.rationale: [src_gould_harvard, src_gould_genomebiology, src_gould_britannica | 1972-2002 | university obituary + science news + encyclopaedia] He developed punctuated equilibrium with fellow student Niles Eldredge, and Lewontin, a friend and colleague of 25 years, says they taught an evolution course together. Two named long-term partnerships are documented, but the sources say little about how he worked with others, so a low-to-moderate confidence.

analytical_rigor.rationale: [src_gould_plos, src_gould_newcriterion, src_gould_harvard | 1978-2011 | specialist critique + critical essay + university obituary] The 2011 PLOS Biology team, who remeasured 308 of Morton's skulls, conclude that most of Gould's criticisms of Morton in his 1978 paper and The Mismeasure of Man are poorly supported and that his own analysis is likely the stronger example of bias, noting he did not remeasure skulls himself; a critical essay quotes Maynard Smith on confused ideas. Against this, Lewontin says he never reduced evolution to a cartoon and Harvard describes complexity-minded scholarship. The case rests mainly on one adversarial post-mortem paper whose rebuttals were not read, and it concerns one famous analysis rather than his whole record, so strong inference at a low confidence, dual-edged.

portrait.reason: No concretely rights-clear portrait found after a second bounded search. Wikidata P18 'Stephen Jay Gould.jpg' (Lawrence Lipke, 1980, 415x564) and the Commons Eric Taylor 1985 Flamingo's Smile jacket image (2920x3544) are tagged Public domain only on the unproven theory that a book dust jacket lacking a copyright notice is PD-US (no registration search recorded; evidence is an eBay listing). The Kathy Chapman photo has no locatable Commons/Flickr page and rests on an emailed permission to post with credit (not a licence). Checked and rejected: Commons Category:Stephen Jay Gould (only signatures, a 1958 yearbook photo, book cover, diagram, and an NSF 1999 press-release text screenshot that contains no photo); all Wikipedia language editions' images (ru uses an AP fair-use photo); Wellcome Collection API (no Gould images); Smithsonian Institution Archives (site returned 403/unavailable, no item verified); George Eastman Museum Arnold Newman 1995 print (rights restricted); Getty Ulf Andersen (licensed); Science Photo Library caricature (copyright). Next step: a written licence from a rights holder, a US Copyright Office registration search showing no registration for the 1980 or 1985 jackets, or a Harvard MCZ/Smithsonian image with stated terms.

provenance.notes: PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE: Wikidata wbgetentities (2026-10-23) for Q180619 returned en label 'Stephen Jay Gould', description 'American biologist and historian of science (1941-2002)', born 1941-09-10, died 2002-05-20, ko label '스티븐 제이 굴드', P18 'Stephen Jay Gould.jpg'; the lead's hint was correct (the Wikidata description differs from the lead's 'paleontologist' framing; Britannica says paleontologist, evolutionary biologist and science writer). SLUG/QID CHECK: no candidate file or src/data-pipeline reference for slug stephen-jay-gould or Q180619 in the roster54 worktree. REGION north_america, nationality US. VOCABULARY: occupations scientist, biologist and writer, fields biology and natural_science, impact domains scientific/literary/educational, tags communicator/theorist/prolific and archetype cross_disciplinary_generalist are existing ids with EN+KO labels; no paleontologist or historian_of_science occupation label exists (gap reported to the lead; 'historian' exists but was not used because it is not his primary identity). ZERO POLITICS: the McLean v. Arkansas testimony, anti-creationism activity and sociobiology political disputes are not scored or carded. DECEASED SUBJECT RULE: nothing is inferred from his illness; the Harvard Gazette and Genome Biology sentences about cancer/mesothelioma and the Gazette's family passage were ignored. EXCLUDED: health, family, Wikipedia/Wikidata. CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Encyclopaedia Britannica 'Stephen Jay Gould' (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Stephen-Jay-Gould), read via an Internet Archive copy. READ (7 cited non-Wikidata sources + portrait records): Britannica, National Science Board 1999 press release (Internet Archive copy plus the Commons image of it), Harvard Gazette obituary, Genome Biology obituary, Lewis et al. 2011 PLOS Biology, The New Criterion essay (opening only; paywalled remainder NOT read). NOT opened: Gould's own books and essays (self material), the Science 1978 paper, the Gould-Lewontin spandrels paper (Royal Society blocked), the New York Times obituary (403), the Guardian obituary (404), later rebuttals of Lewis et al., Dawkins and Dennett's own critiques, McLean v. Arkansas materials. Maynard Smith's judgement is known only through the New Criterion's quotation, so it is used only as a named-critic note and caps the independent_thinking and analytical_rigor confidence. PERSPECTIVES: encyclopaedia; award body (NSB); university obituary with named colleagues (Lewontin, Knoll); science news; specialist adversarial critique (Lewis et al.); critical opinion essay. COUNTER-VOICES: Wilson (Britannica), Maynard Smith (New Criterion quote), Lewis et al. on the Morton analysis. CALIBRATION: praise is retrospective and obituary-based, so the highest score is 72 and the highest confidence 0.60; eight rows, no padding. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed creative_originality (lowered 76/0.66 to 72/0.60: retrospective awards, shared credit, contested), persuasiveness (lowered 74/0.60 to 70/0.55: admiring obituaries and indirect measure) and analytical_rigor (kept low at 55/0.38: single adversarial paper, rebuttals unread; flagged for the lead). BROAD FLAG: behavioural depth is thin because most sources are obituaries; the lead may want a direct read of a biography (e.g. Ruse or Sulloway) or the Eldredge account before relying on collaboration or conflict_tolerance. PORTRAIT: HELD; see portrait.reason. Candidate remains evidence_approved with portrait held per the brief.
